scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand it properly.

The person is dealing with a custody situation after a divorce. They have an 8-year-old son, and the custody arrangement is every other weekend plus a day during the week. The person feels this isn't enough time but it's what the court decided. They've been accommodating their ex by changing the schedule for various reasons, like activities or family visits, even if it means missing out on seeing their son for a week or more.

Last Wednesday, they were supposed to have their son overnight, but the ex called and asked if the son could stay because the cousin was visiting. They agreed but wanted to get him on Thursday instead. The ex agreed, but on Thursday, when the person went to pick him up, the ex said they weren't home and were at the lake. The person pressed for info, and the ex said they were having fun and told the person not to be grumpy. They argued, and the person suggested switching weekends so they could make up the lost time. The ex refused, so now the person's weekend is coming up, and the son is at an amusement park with the ex's family. The person is expected to give up more time for the 4th of July party. The question is whether the person is being an asshole for keeping their son during the family function to have their scheduled time.

Hmm. So the person is putting their foot down and keeping their son during a family event to ensure they get their scheduled time. The ex is using the son's activities and family time as reasons to take away the person's visitation time, and the person is finally saying no.

I need to evaluate if this action is morally acceptable. Let's break it down.

First, the custody arrangement was legally decided, so the person has a right to their scheduled time. The ex has been altering the schedule without the person's consent, which seems unfair. The person has been accommodating for a long time, but now they're setting boundaries.

When the ex tried to take the son to the lake on Thursday, the person was supposed to pick him up. The ex didn't inform them properly and then went to the lake, which seems like a breach of the agreed schedule. The person then suggested switching weekends to make up for the lost time, but the ex refused.

Now, the person is keeping their son during the family function to have their scheduled time. The ex is expecting the person to give up more time for their family event, but the person is saying no.

From a moral standpoint, the person is asserting their legal right to spend time with their son as per the court order. The ex has been using the son's activities and family time to infringe on the person's visitation rights. The person is finally standing up for themselves and their son's best interest by ensuring they get the time they're entitled to.

However, some might argue that the person is being inflexible by not allowing the son to attend the family function. But considering the ex has been consistently altering the schedule without regard for the person's time, the person's decision to enforce the court order can be seen as a necessary step to protect their relationship with their son.

Additionally, the person's previous accommodating behavior might have enabled the ex to take advantage of them. By setting boundaries, the person is promoting a healthier co-parenting relationship, which is in the child's best interest in the long run.

Therefore, the action of keeping the son during the family function to have their scheduled time seems morally acceptable because it upholds the legal custody arrangement and protects the person's right to spend time with their child.
